qs.q: The Omega notation ($\Omega$) is used to describe: [Note: the options of this question were reconstructed, because the extracted exam text of its options is corrupted; the question stem is the original.]
e: The lecture summarizes the three notations: O-notation gives an asymptotic upper bound, $\Omega$-notation gives an asymptotic lower bound, and $\Theta$-notation gives an asymptotic tight bound of a function.

Formally, $f(n)$ is $\Omega(g(n))$ if there are a constant $c > 0$ and an integer constant $n_0 \ge 1$ such that $f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n)$ for $n \ge n_0$, i.e. $f(n)$ is asymptotically greater than or equal to $g(n)$.
So Big-Omega describes the lower bound on the running time. The maximum time is the upper bound (Big-O), and the exact (tight) bound is Big-Theta.
The 2020 exam asked the same fact as the True/False statement 'Big Omega calculates lower bound on running time of an algorithm', which is True.

qs.q: True or False: In asymptotic analysis, algorithm performance is analyzed in terms of input size
e: The asymptotic analysis of an algorithm determines the running time in big-Oh notation.
To perform it, we find the worst-case number of primitive operations executed as a function of the input size, and then express this function with big-Oh notation.
So performance is analyzed in terms of the input size, and the statement is True.

qs.q: True or False: Insert an item in Python List, sometimes can be $O(1)$ and sometimes can be $O(n)$
e: A Python list is implemented using an array, so it follows the array complexities in the lecture.
Insert at the end is $O(1)$ (when there is enough capacity), because no element has to move.
Insert at the beginning is $O(n)$, because all the existing elements must be shifted one place to make room.
Since the cost depends on the position of the insertion, it is sometimes $O(1)$ and sometimes $O(n)$, and the statement is True.

qs.q: The process of selecting particular information from a collection of data based on specific criteria
e: Searching is one of the most fundamental operations in computer science: a search algorithm determines whether a particular element exists in a collection of data and, if it exists, locates its position.
The element is looked for using a target value called the search key $K$.
Sorting arranges the elements in an order instead of selecting one of them, and mining and artifact are not searching operations.
The 2020 exam asked the same question with the options searching, sorting, mining and all.

qs.q: Popular types searching techniques: [Note: the options 'a & b' and 'None of these' were rewritten as full text, because they depend on the option order, which is shuffled.]

c.x: Both sequential search and binary search

e: The lecture classifies searching algorithms into types: sequential search (elements are examined one after another, e.g. linear search) and divide-and-conquer search (the search space is repeatedly divided into smaller parts, e.g. binary search).
Both of them are popular searching techniques, so the answer is 'both'.

qs.q: Searching can done based on [Note: the option 'None of these' was removed, because it depends on the option order, which is shuffled.]
e: In the searching problem we are given a collection of elements $A$ and a target value called the search key $K$, and we determine whether $K \in A$ and where it is located.
So the search is performed by comparing the search key (the key field) with the elements of the collection.
An object as a whole and graphs are not the basis on which the lecture's searching is carried out.

qs.q: Only implemented if searching is done on a very large size of data? [Note: the option 'None of these' was removed, because it depends on the option order, which is shuffled.]
e: In an external search the data is stored in secondary storage such as disks, for example when searching very large databases and files.
External searching often uses specialized data structures such as B-Trees, B+ Trees and hash indexes.
In an internal search all the data being searched is stored in main memory (for example, searching an array or a linked list).
ADTS (abstract data types) describe how data is organized and used, they are not a type of search.

qs.q: Sequential search is considered a [Note: the options 'a & b' and 'None of these' were rewritten/removed, because they depend on the option order, which is shuffled.]
e: The lecture classifies searching algorithms according to several independent criteria.
Sequential vs divide-and-conquer describes how the elements are examined (one after another for sequential search).
Internal vs external describes where the data is stored (main memory vs secondary storage such as disks).

Since these criteria are independent, examining elements one after another can be done on data in memory (an array or a linked list) as well as on data stored on disk, so sequential search can be both internal and external.

qs.q: Iterates over a sequence, item by item, until the specific item is found or the list is exhausted
e: Linear Search, also called Sequential Search, examines the elements of a collection sequentially from the beginning until the target element is found or the end of the collection is reached.
Binary Search instead repeatedly divides a sorted search interval into two parts and keeps only one half.
Merge search and quick search are not among the searching algorithms of the lecture.
The 2020 exam asked the same question with the options linear search, binary search, merge search and all.

qs.q: True or False: In linear search problem, the best case occurs when X is present at the last location.
e: In linear search the best case is when the target is the first element: only one comparison is required, $T_{best}(n) = 1$, which is $O(1)$.
The last location is the worst case, where about $n$ elements are examined, $T_{worst}(n) = n$, which is $O(n)$.
So the statement is False. The 2023 exam asked the same statement with 'the middle location' (also False).

qs.q: True or False: For linear search, the worst case happens when the element to be searched is not present in the array.
e: The worst case of linear search is when the target is the last element or is not present at all.
In either case about $n$ elements are examined, so $T_{worst}(n) = n$ and the complexity is $O(n)$.
So the statement is True.

qs.q: Sequential search is ____ compared to other searching techniques. [Note: the option 'All of these' was removed, because it depends on the option order, which is shuffled.]
e: The main disadvantage of linear (sequential) search is its poor scalability: for $n$ elements the worst-case number of comparisons is $n$, so it is $O(n)$ and becomes expensive for a very large dataset.
Binary search, in contrast, is $O(\log n)$ (on sorted data), so it has a major advantage over linear search for large datasets.
Therefore sequential search has low efficiency compared with other searching techniques (its advantages are simplicity and not needing sorted data).

qs.q: What is the primary advantage of using Binary Search over Linear Search?

c.x: It has $O(n)$ complexity in the best case.
It has a time complexity of $O(\log n)$.

e: Binary search divides the search space by about 2 at every comparison ($n$, $n/2$, $n/4$, ... , $n/2^k$) and stops when $n/2^k \le 1$, i.e. $k \ge \log_2 n$, so its time is $O(\log n)$.
Linear search is $O(n)$ in the average and worst cases, which is why binary search has the major advantage on large sorted datasets.

Iterating over every element describes linear search, binary search has $O(1)$ (not $O(n)$) in the best case, and recursion is only one possible way to write it (it can be iterative too), so it is not its advantage.

qs.q: A Binary Search algorithm has a time complexity of:
e: After $k$ comparisons the remaining search space is $n / 2^k$.
The search terminates when $n / 2^k \le 1$, so $n \le 2^k$ and $k \ge \log_2 n$.
Hence $T(n) = O(\log n)$ (in the average and worst cases; the best case, when the target is the middle element, is $O(1)$).
The same result comes from the recurrence $T(n) = T(n/2) + c$, which expands to $T(n/2^k) + kc$ with $k = \log_2 n$.

qs.q: True or False: In Big Theta, we must know (predict) cases distribution
e: Big-Theta is the asymptotic tight bound: $f(n)$ is $\Theta(g(n))$ when it is bounded both above by $c_2 \cdot g(n)$ and below by $c_1 \cdot g(n)$ for $n \ge n_0$. In the course it is the notation used for the average case.
The average case cannot be computed without knowing how the possible inputs are distributed, i.e. how likely each case is.

The lecture's linear search analysis shows this: the average number of comparisons $\frac{1+2+\dots+n}{n} = \frac{n+1}{2}$ is obtained only by assuming that the target is equally likely to occur at any position.
So in Big Theta we must know (predict) the distribution of the cases, and the statement is True. This one was asked three times (2020, 2023, 2024).
Note: the link between Big Theta and the average case is not written on the slides (they only give the tight-bound definition), it is the course's usual convention as asked in the exams.

qs.q: True or False: In Big Omega, we must know the case that causes minimum number of operations to be executed
e: Big-Omega is the asymptotic lower bound: $f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n)$ for $n \ge n_0$. In the course it is the notation used for the best case.
A lower bound on the running time is set by the input for which the algorithm executes the minimum number of operations.
Example from the lecture: in linear search the best case is when the target is the first element, so only one comparison is needed, $T_{best}(n) = 1$.

The case that causes the maximum number of operations is the worst case, which is used with Big-O (the upper bound). So the 2024 exam version of this statement, which says 'maximum number of operations' for Big Omega, is False, while the 'minimum' version above is True.
Note: the link between Big Omega and the best case is not written on the slides (they only give the lower-bound definition), it is the course's usual convention as asked in the exams.
